note.explanation: Every measurement has some uncertainty, because an instrument cannot measure beyond the precision allowed by its smallest division. For an analogue scale, the maximum uncertainty is usually half the smallest division. Repeated readings and an average can reduce uncertainty.
examples: A metre rule has a smallest division of 0.1 cm, so the maximum uncertainty is ±0.05 cm.
If a digital instrument's last digit fluctuates, that fluctuation shows uncertainty in the reading.
note.simple: A measurement is not perfectly exact. The instrument limits how certain the reading can be.
note.checkQuestion: A scale has a smallest division of 0.1 cm. What is the maximum uncertainty?
note.title: Uncertainty in a Measurement
steps: For the metre-rule example, divide 0.1 cm by 2.
State the maximum uncertainty as ±0.05 cm.
note.answer: For a metre rule with 0.1 cm smallest divisions, the maximum uncertainty is ±0.05 cm.

mcqs.stem: A metre rule has a smallest division of 0.1 cm. What is the maximum uncertainty in a reading?
rationales: This is the full smallest division, not half of it.
The maximum uncertainty is half the smallest division: 0.1 cm ÷ 2 = 0.05 cm.
This is smaller than half the smallest division.
This is greater than the smallest division of the rule.

mcqs.stem: What sets a limit to the accuracy that can be achieved with a measuring instrument?
rationales: The smallest division of the instrument limits the degree of accuracy possible.
The object's mass does not determine the instrument's scale resolution.
The total length of the scale does not set the precision of each reading.
The number of readings can help reduce uncertainty but does not set the instrument's scale limit.

mcqs.stem: On a digital instrument, uncertainty is often shown by fluctuation in which part of the reading?
rationales: The first digit is not usually the digit that fluctuates to show uncertainty.
The last digit commonly fluctuates and indicates the uncertain part of the digital reading.
A unit symbol does not fluctuate as part of the measured value.
The textbook describes fluctuation in the last digit, not equal changes in every digit.

options: Take several readings and find their average
mcqs.stem: How can uncertainty in a short time interval be reduced?
rationales: One reading does not use repeated measurements to reduce uncertainty.
Taking multiple readings and finding the average can reduce uncertainty.
Rounding every reading up introduces a bias rather than reducing uncertainty.
Changing the unit does not itself reduce uncertainty.

mcqs.stem: Which activity is excluded from the textbook's statement that measurements have inevitable uncertainty?
rationales: The text says uncertainty applies whenever a physical quantity is measured except counting.
A wire's diameter is measured and can have uncertainty.
A time interval is measured and can have uncertainty.
A length is measured and can have uncertainty.

options: They show the uncertainty or accuracy of a measured quantity conveniently
They remove all uncertainty from a measurement
They change the instrument's smallest division
They are used only for digital instruments
mcqs.stem: Why are significant figures useful in measurements?
rationales: The textbook says significant figures conveniently indicate uncertainty or accuracy in a measured value.
Significant figures do not make any measurement perfectly certain.
Writing significant figures does not change the instrument's scale.
Significant figures are not restricted to digital instruments.

yourTurn.question:
State the number of significant digits in each measurement.
(a) 0.0045 m (b) 2.047 m (c) 3.40 m (d) 3.420 × 10⁴ m
solution: (a) In 0.0045 m, the significant digits are 4 and 5: 2 significant digits.
(b) In 2.047 m, the zero between non-zero digits counts: 4 significant digits.
(c) In 3.40 m, the final zero after the decimal point counts: 3 significant digits.
(d) In 3.420 × 10⁴ m, count the digits in 3.420: 4 significant digits.

steps.why: The smallest division is 0.1 cm, so its midpoint divides it into two equal parts.
steps.text: The metre rule is calibrated in millimetres, so its smallest division is 0.1 cm.

steps.why: The end of the line lies between the 10.3 cm and 10.4 cm marks, so the reading is decided by its position relative to the midpoint.
steps.text: If the end does not touch or cross the midpoint, record the previous division; if it touches or has crossed the midpoint, record the next division.

steps.why: The maximum uncertainty is half of the smallest division.

example.question: A straight line is measured with a metre rule calibrated in millimetres. Its end lies between 10.3 cm and 10.4 cm. How is the reading chosen, and what is the maximum uncertainty?
example.answer: Choose the previous or next division according to whether the endpoint is before or at/past the midpoint. The maximum uncertainty is ±0.05 cm.

explain.title: Measurements are not perfect
explain.body: There is no such thing as a perfect measurement. Whenever a physical quantity is measured except counting, there is inevitably some uncertainty about its determined value due to some instrument. The instrument's smallest division limits how accurately you can read it.

explain.title: Uncertainty on an analogue scale
explain.body: For the metre-rule example, the smallest division is 0.1 cm. The maximum uncertainty is half of this, or ±0.05 cm. Use the midpoint convention: record the previous division if the endpoint is before the midpoint, and the next division if it touches or crosses the midpoint.

explain.title: Digital readings and repeated readings
explain.body: With digital scale, this is reflected in fluctuation of the last digit. For small lengths or short time intervals, take multiple readings and find their average to reduce uncertainty.

explain.title: Significant figures
explain.body: The uncertainty or accuracy in the value of a measured quantity can be indicated conveniently by using significant figures.

mistakes: Using the whole smallest division instead of half of it when stating the maximum uncertainty.
Ignoring the midpoint convention when deciding whether to record the previous or next division.
Treating every digit on a digital display as equally certain instead of noticing fluctuation in the last digit.
Using just one reading when several readings and their average could reduce uncertainty.
Counting leading zeros as significant digits.
